rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate all six compounds while minimizing the risk of non-elution. The retention window and critical resolutions will guide subsequent adjustments to gradient slope, solvent range, and temperature.
The maximum CRF is already achieved, with ample resolution margin. Shorten the gradient to test a faster fully resolved method while retaining injection 1 as the proven optimum-score fallback.

Shorten the gradient one grid step to seek a faster method with the same maximum CRF. The current minimum resolution of 2.46 provides some margin, but the earliest pair will likely approach the 1.5 threshold.

Injection 3 retains the maximum CRF with a shorter elution time, but its critical pair has little resolution margin. Test higher temperature at the same gradient to assess whether faster elution and favorable selectivity can coexist.

Higher temperature worsened the critical early pair, so test the lowest temperature to favor its separation while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This probes whether temperature selectivity can compensate for gradient compression; injection 3 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Reduce the gradient slope while retaining the two-minute ramp and low temperature, aiming to raise the critical early-pair resolution above 1.5. The lower final organic fraction may delay the last peak, but this tests a potentially faster fully resolved alternative to injection 3.

Shift the solvent window upward while preserving injection 6’s gradient slope to accelerate the late peak. Test whether the critical early pair retains R ≥ 1.5 despite the higher starting organic fraction.

Shift the solvent window upward another step at the same slope and temperature, since the previous shift preserved critical-pair resolution. This should accelerate the last peak while testing whether full resolution is maintained.

Raise both gradient endpoints while preserving the slope that has maintained full resolution across three runs. This tests the highest final organic fraction for faster late-peak elution, with particular attention to compression of the early pair.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to accelerate elution while slightly reducing the gradient slope. Monitor the early pair for loss of retention near the dead-time region; injection 9 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Raise the starting organic fraction another step to seek faster elution while retaining the maximum CRF. The early-pair resolution improved in injection 10, but proximity to the dead time makes further compression a risk worth testing.

Back off to the last fully resolved starting composition and raise temperature by one step to seek faster late-peak elution. Injection 10’s minimum resolution of 1.77 provides limited margin for the temperature-induced loss of early-pair selectivity.

Test one further temperature step to locate the speed–resolution boundary around injection 12, the fastest proven maximum-CRF method. The early pair may fall below 1.5, in which case 30 C remains the preferred temperature for this gradient.

Return to the last fully resolved temperature and slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the critical-pair margin. This tests a lower-solvent-strength, potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative, accepting some delay of the last peak.

Shift injection 12’s solvent window down one step at the same slope to test whether greater early retention improves the critical-pair margin. The maximum CRF is already secured; this probes a nearby fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 12 as the fastest proven method.

Combine the better early-pair selectivity at 25 C with a slightly shallower gradient to seek additional resolution margin in a short maximum-CRF method. Injection 12 remains the fastest proven fully resolved option.

Shift injection 16’s solvent window downward at the same slope to test whether keeping both early peaks farther from the dead time improves resolution margin. This explores a more robust maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Test whether injection 17’s shallower gradient and greater early retention can support 35 C without losing full resolution. This probes temperature–gradient compensation, while injection 12 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Back off one temperature step from injection 18 to recover full resolution in this solvent window. This should offer more early-pair margin than injection 15, while injection 12 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Test the intermediate solvent window between injections 9 and 17 to balance rapid late-peak elution with extra critical-pair resolution margin. Injection 12 remains the fastest proven method attaining the maximum CRF.

Test the remaining lower-starting-composition neighbor of injection 12 to check whether full resolution survives with greater early retention and the strongest final solvent. This directly tests the local boundary around the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Refine around injection 16 by lowering the final organic fraction one step, testing whether a shallower gradient adds critical-pair resolution margin while keeping elution near three minutes. Injection 12 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.
Raise injection 22’s temperature one step to shorten elution while testing whether its improved resolution margin preserves maximum CRF. Injection 12 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Test one lower starting-organic step from injection 9 to define the full-resolution boundary at the strongest endpoint and lowest temperature. Injection 12 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method; this candidate checks an alternative with greater early retention.

Lower the final organic fraction one step from injection 24 to improve its marginal early-pair resolution while retaining a short run. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 12 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.
